title: Design of Everyday Things: Screens That Explain Themselves
summary: Don Norman's Design of Everyday Things, read for software teams: discoverability, signifiers, mapping, feedback and the mental model your screens teach users.
author: Nguyen Le Phong

book.title: The Design of Everyday Things
book.originalTitle: The Design of Everyday Things; originally published as The Psychology of Everyday Things
book.note: A reading of the 2013 revised and expanded edition, mostly chapters 1 to 3, through the lens of software and product work. It is not a chapter-by-chapter summary.

html:
Your first morning at a new job, you walk up to the office coffee machine. Four silver buttons, same size, no labels you can read without your glasses. You press one. Nothing happens for three seconds, so you press it again. Now the machine is running a cleaning cycle and there's hot water on the counter. Nobody laughs at you, but somebody does say, "Oh yeah, everyone does that once."

"Everyone does that once" is the whole of Don Norman's The Design of Everyday Things in four words. When lots of smart people make the same mistake, the design is the thing that's broken. Norman tells the story with doors, stoves and fridges. The same failures show up on every screen we ship: buttons that don't say what they do, actions with no visible result, settings nobody can predict.

About the book

This post draws on the revised and expanded edition of The Design of Everyday Things (Basic Books, 2013). It first came out in 1988 as The Psychology of Everyday Things. I mostly use chapters 1 to 3 here and read them with software in mind. Chapter 5, on human error, gets its own post: When "Human Error" Is Really a Design Problem.

Can people tell what to do, and what it means?

Chapter 1 opens with two questions Norman treats as the core of good design. Discoverability: can people figure out which actions are possible, and where and how to do them? Understanding: what does it all mean, and what do the controls and settings actually do? A screen can pass every test and still fail both.

Take an internal refund screen. To the team that built it, the flow is obvious: find the order, pick a reason, type an amount, hit Submit. A support agent seeing it for the first time has other questions. Full refund or partial? Does the customer get an email? Can I undo this? Does finance see it automatically? If the screen doesn't answer those at the moment of the click, the agent answers them from memory, from a Slack thread, or by crossing their fingers.

The fix is mostly words and layout. Make the main button say "Refund $48.20 to Visa ending 4242" instead of "Submit". Put a small summary next to it: customer gets an email, finance gets notified, you can cancel this for the next 30 minutes, this note goes into the audit log. Nothing about the backend changed, and the agent now knows what will happen before it happens.

Expert tools get a little more slack here, but only a little. A database migration console is allowed to be complicated. It shouldn't be mysterious.

Signifiers: the hints that say what's possible

Norman borrowed the word "affordance" for his 1988 book and then watched designers use it for everything. In a 2008 essay he pushed a different word: "Forget affordances: what people need, and what design must provide, are signifiers" (Signifiers, not affordances). An affordance is what you can do with something. A signifier is the cue that tells you so. A door affords pushing; the flat metal plate is the signifier that tells you to push. The 2013 edition gives signifiers their own section in chapter 1.

On a screen, signifiers are labels, the shape of a button, a cursor that changes on hover, a disabled state, a placeholder, an empty state that tells you what goes there, even where something sits on the page. Norman also points out that a signifier works whether or not anyone meant it to. If your card has a drop shadow like every clickable card in your app, people will try to click it.

The trap is mistaking a clean mockup for a clear screen. Labels get cut, secondary actions move behind icons, contrast drops, and the design review loves it. Then real users show up, hover over things at random, open menus just to see what's inside, and ask support where the export button went.

Weak signifierWhat the user is thinkingA clearer move
Disabled Submit with no reasonIs the page broken, or did I miss a field?Say what's missing, right next to the field that needs it.
Icon-only deleteDoes this delete it, archive it, or just hide it?Add a text label, give it more visual weight and offer a way back.
Clickable card that looks like plain contentCan I open this, select it, or only read it?Hover and focus states, a pointer cursor and a visible action area.
Toggle with vague copyWhat changes when I turn this on?Describe the concrete behavior and show the new state after the change.

Take a billing setting called "Smart retry". The engineers know it means a failed payment gets retried three times over seven days. The customer has no idea. A better setting says what happens, when, whether the customer is told, and how to switch it off. That copy is part of how the feature behaves, so it deserves the same care as the retry logic.

Mapping: put the control near what it changes

Mapping is the link between a control and its effect. Norman's favorite example is the stove. Four burners in a square, four knobs in a row, and you're reading tiny diagrams every time you cook. Lay the knobs out in the same pattern as the burners and nobody needs a diagram. He calls this natural mapping: use spatial analogy so the layout explains itself, like putting the light switches for a big room in the same arrangement as the lights.

Software has the same problem, just harder to see. A dashboard with filters on top and charts below works because you change the filter and watch the chart right under it move. Now think about a permissions screen where checkboxes on the left change a preview hidden in a tab on the right. The code is fine. The person clicking has no way to connect what they did with what happened.

Deploy screens are where this gets serious. If production and staging look nearly the same, someone will eventually deploy to the wrong one. Put production in its own clearly labeled area, make the version you're about to ship visible right on the button, and the screen starts doing some of the remembering for the person under pressure.

A question for your next design review

When someone changes this control, can they see right away which part of the system changed, what state it's in now, and how to undo it if they got it wrong?

Feedback: tell people you heard them

Norman is blunt about feedback in chapter 1. It has to be immediate, and he says even a tenth of a second of delay can feel off. It has to be informative: a beep tells you something happened but not what, or what to do next. And it has to be planned and prioritized, because too much feedback is its own failure. His dishwasher beeps at 3 a.m. to say it's done, which rather defeats the point of running it overnight.

Jakob Nielsen's response-time limits line up with this: about 0.1 seconds feels instant, about 1 second keeps your flow of thought, and past about 10 seconds people need a progress indicator or they drift off (Nielsen Norman Group). In chapter 2 Norman frames the same problem as the gulf of evaluation: the gap between what the system did and what the person can tell it did (The Two UX Gulfs).

A payment form shows the gulf nicely. You press "Pay" and the page just sits there. The button still looks clickable. Did it go through? Do you press again? A good form disables the button at once, shows progress, says not to close the tab, and lands on a clear final state. If it fails, the error says what happened, whether any money moved, and what's safe to do next. A lot of duplicate charge tickets start with a screen that went silent at the wrong moment.

Your internal tools deserve the same treatment. A CI page that only says "failed" makes you dig. One that names the stage, the failing check and the log line saves the next person ten minutes. A feature flag console that only says "Saved" should say which environment changed and when the new value takes effect. These feel like polish until it's late, everyone's tired, and the release is due in an hour.

Conceptual models: the story people tell themselves

Everyone using your product carries a rough story of how it works. Norman calls it a conceptual model. It doesn't need to be accurate, just good enough to predict what happens next. When it's wrong, careful people make wrong moves.

His example in chapter 1 is a fridge he used to own. Two compartments, two dials, one labeled "freezer" and one labeled "fresh food". Anyone would assume each dial controls its own compartment. Wrong. There was one thermostat and one cooling unit: one dial set the temperature, the other decided how the cold air was split between the two sections. So each dial changed both compartments, and Norman found it almost impossible to get the temperatures right. The labels taught a false model, and careful use couldn't fix that.

The designer can't sit next to every user and explain. Everything the user learns comes from what Norman calls the system image: the product itself, its labels, docs, help pages, error messages. For Norman, all communication between designer and user goes through that image. So if your product says "workspace" on one page, "organization" on another and "team" in billing, users don't just learn three words. They may build three different models and never know which one controls permissions or who owns the data.

AreaConfusing modelClearer model
Publishing drafts"Saved", "submitted" and "published" appear as loose labels in different places.One visible path: draft, in review, scheduled, live, archived.
Team permissionsRoles, seats and billing owner all mixed on one screen.Access, billing and ownership in separate sections, with a line on how they relate.
Data importYou upload a file and wait with no idea whether it passed validation.Upload, validate, map columns, preview, commit and roll back as separate visible steps.

This is why naming and states belong in design review, not only in code review. The interface is teaching people how your product works. Teach a messy story and people act on a messy story.

Put the knowledge in the world

Chapter 3 asks how people behave precisely when what they remember is fuzzy. Norman's answer: they don't need perfect memory, because a lot of what they need is out in the world, in the layout, the labels and the constraints. Knowledge in the head is fast once learned. Knowledge in the world is there when you need it, so nobody has to learn it first.

In software that looks very ordinary. Keep field requirements visible instead of revealing them after a failed submit. Show an example next to an input. Keep a step indicator on a multi-step flow. Show recent changes next to a risky setting. Nobody should have to remember from last month that the CSV import wants dates as 2026-11-17. Put a sample row on the screen and validate before upload.

It matters most for tools people use under pressure: incident consoles, finance workflows, production deploys. People using those are interrupted, tired and juggling three things. Every rule the screen holds for them is one less thing they can forget at 2 a.m.

Try this week

  • Pick one screen your team owns and ask a new teammate to use it while you watch without helping. Write down every place they hesitate.
  • Find one button that says "Submit", "OK" or "Save" before something risky and rewrite it to say what will happen.
  • List every name your product uses for the same concept (workspace, org, team) and pick one.
  • Check one slow action: does it give feedback within a second, and a progress hint if it takes longer than ten?
  • Move one rule people keep asking about from a wiki page onto the screen where they need it.

The habit I'd keep from this book is the reaction when someone gets confused. Before "how did they miss that?", ask what the screen failed to say. Usually the answer is one missing label, one silent state, one control too far from its effect. Each of those is a small fix, and you can ship one this week.

faqs.q: What is discoverability in UX design?
faqs.a: In The Design of Everyday Things, Don Norman defines discoverability as whether people can figure out which actions are possible, and where and how to do them. He pairs it with understanding: knowing what the controls and settings mean. A screen with hidden actions or unlabeled controls fails discoverability even when the code works.

faqs.q: What is the difference between an affordance and a signifier?
faqs.a: An affordance is what you can do with something. A signifier is the cue that tells you so, like a label, a button shape, a cursor change or a disabled state. In his 2008 essay 'Signifiers, not affordances', Norman argued that designers should focus on signifiers, because people act on the cues they can see.

faqs.q: How fast should an interface give feedback?
faqs.a: Norman writes that feedback must be immediate and that even a tenth of a second of delay can feel off. Nielsen Norman Group's response-time limits say about 0.1 seconds feels instant, about 1 second keeps the user's flow of thought, and past about 10 seconds people need a progress indicator.

faqs.q: What is a conceptual model in design?
faqs.a: It's the rough story a person has in their head about how a product works. Users build it from the system image: the product, its labels, docs and messages. If names, states and flows contradict each other, users build the wrong model and make wrong moves even when they're careful.
